hints: Count the total electrons for Co (Z = 27) and remember the order of filling after argon is $4s$ before $3d$, but think carefully about which electrons are lost first when forming a 2+ ion.
walkthrough:
Build the cobalt atom from argon**
Cobalt has atomic number 27, so start from $1s^22s^22p^6$ given and add the rest. Argon accounts for 18 electrons, leaving 9 more. Fill $4s$ with 2 electrons first, then $3d$ with 7 electrons. That gives $...3s^23p^63d^74s^2$.

Form Co2+ by removing 4s first**
A very common slip is to remove $3d$ electrons. Always remove the $4s$ electrons first when a transition metal ionises, because $4s$ is higher in energy once the atom is formed. So remove both $4s$ electrons and leave $...3s^23p^63d^7$ with no $4s$ electrons.

hints: Recall the familiar colour of aqueous cobalt(II) nitrate before any chloride is added, think of the hexaaqua ion with water ligands.
Think about what happens when a very high concentration of chloride ligands is present and how water ligands can be replaced.
Recall the classic test tube observation for cobalt with concentrated HCl, what is the new intense colour formed?
Write the formulae for the start and end complexes, paying attention to coordination number, ligand charge and overall complex charge.
Compare the coordination numbers 6 and 4 and link each to its usual geometry for cobalt(II).
walkthrough:
Picture the starting solution**
In water, $\text{Co}^{2+}$ exists as the hexaaquacobalt(II) ion, $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$. Six water molecules surround the central cobalt. This complex is octahedral and gives the familiar pink solution.

Follow the ligand exchange**
Concentrated $\text{HCl}$ provides a huge excess of $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands. Chloride replaces water in a ligand substitution:
$$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
High $[\text{Cl}^-]$ drives the equilibrium to the right.

Link colour change to new complex**
The tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion, $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, is an intense blue. So you see pink turning to blue. The change in ligand and in geometry changes the d-orbital splitting, so different wavelengths of light are absorbed.

Assign geometries**
$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ has coordination number 6, so octahedral. $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ has coordination number 4 with a relatively large $\text{Co}^{2+}$ and large $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands, so tetrahedral. Check charges: $+2 + 4(-1) = -2$, consistent with $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$.

Final answer: Initial solution is pink due to $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, octahedral.
On addition of conc. HCl it turns blue due to $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, tetrahedral.

hints: Note the coordination number is 4 in both $\text{Co}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$ and $\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$, but only one of them shows two isomers, think about which geometry allows cis and trans positions.
Recall that tetrahedral arrangement places all four positions equivalent, so swapping two ligands gives the same structure, while square planar has distinct adjacent and opposite positions.
Sketch how two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ and two $\text{I}$ ligands can be arranged around Ni in a square plane in two different ways, and around Co in a tetrahedron in only one way.
walkthrough:
Use isomer count to assign geometry**
Both formulae are $\text{ML}_2\text{X}_2$ with coordination number 4. Tetrahedral gives only one structure because every corner of a tetrahedron is adjacent to every other corner. Square planar gives two structures, cis and trans. Since Ni shows two isomers, Ni must be square planar. Since Co shows only one, Co must be tetrahedral.

Draw the cobalt complex**
Place Co at the centre of a tetrahedron. Draw wedged and dashed bonds to show 3D shape, with one $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ and one $\text{I}$ on solid wedges and the other $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ and $\text{I}$ on hashed wedges, or simply show four bonds in tetrahedral fashion. Any arrangement is identical, so one diagram is enough.

Draw the two nickel isomers**
Place Ni at the centre of a square. For cis-$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$, put the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands on adjacent corners (for example top left and top right) and the two $\text{I}$ ligands on the other two adjacent corners. For trans-$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$, put the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands opposite each other (for example left and right) and the two $\text{I}$ ligands opposite each other (top and bottom). Label clearly which is cis and which is trans.

Final answer: $\text{Co}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$: tetrahedral with Co at centre, two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ and two $\text{I}$ at tetrahedral corners, only one possible arrangement.
$\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{I}_2$: square planar, cis isomer has the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ adjacent (90 degrees) and the two $\text{I}$ adjacent; trans isomer has the two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ opposite (180 degrees) and the two $\text{I}$ opposite.
